item.title: Shoulder Rotation MET — Gentle Isometric Trial
clinicalUse: A patient tries to rotate the shoulder outward to put on a jacket. The arm stops at a comfortable limit; you check whether the problem is irritability, weakness, capsular restriction or another source.
A low-effort shoulder-rotation MET variation may be explored in a medically appropriate and well-screened presentation, alongside active rehabilitation.
Retest external-rotation range in the same supported position and the patient's dressing-related task.
patientPosition: Supine with the shoulder comfortably close to the side and the elbow flexed around 90°, a small towel supporting the upper arm as needed.
Only move toward the first comfortable external-rotation barrier; do not force an apprehensive or unstable shoulder.
therapistPosition: Stand beside the shoulder, supporting the elbow with one hand and controlling the distal forearm with the other.
Keep your own arm position secure so resistance can be matched gently rather than applied in a sudden jerk.
stabilization: Stabilize the upper arm against unwanted abduction and the trunk against rotation while preserving comfort.
Do not pin down a shoulder that becomes guarded or painful.
contact: One hand supports the elbow/upper arm, the other gives broad contact at distal forearm for gentle resisted internal-rotation intent.
Avoid torque directly at the wrist, painful pressure at the bicipital groove, or loading through an unstable joint.
forceDirection: With the shoulder near the comfortable external-rotation limit, ask for a gentle internal-rotation effort against matched isometric resistance (roughly toward the abdomen, without actual joint movement).
After full relaxation, cautiously re-explore only the available comfortable external-rotation range. Technique choice depends on the impairment and the patient's response.
dosage: A teaching starting point can be 3–5 low-effort holds of around 3–6 seconds with easy breathing and sufficient relaxation; this is not a universally validated optimum.
Stop or reduce effort if pain or apprehension rises, and reassess before another repetition.
steps: Measure comfortable shoulder external rotation and a functional movement such as reaching into a jacket.
Check instability/apprehension, traumatic injury, post-operative precautions and neurological status.
Support the elbow near the side, gently find the first comfortable external-rotation limit and explain the task.
Ask the patient to push very gently toward internal rotation while you match the effort without allowing movement.
Hold briefly at low effort with breathing relaxed, then ask for a complete release.
Reassess the new comfortable external-rotation range without forcing end range.
Repeat only if comfortable and useful, then train active rotator-cuff/scapular control.
reassess: Active and supported external rotation in a consistent position
Tolerance during targeted active external-rotation exercise
mistakes: Resisting with maximal force because the word 'energy' sounds powerful.
Letting the shoulder translate or the trunk twist rather than producing a gentle isometric effort.
Claiming a brief contraction permanently corrected a capsular restriction.
safety: Do not use forceful end-range rotation in anterior instability, recent dislocation or acute trauma.
Respect post-operative limits, fracture concern, severe inflammation and marked apprehension.
Stop for neurological symptoms, sharp pain or worsening instability sensation.
item.visualCue: Support elbow at side → gentle isometric internal-rotation effort → relax → retest external rotation.

story.title: The jacket that refuses to cooperate
story.scene: A patient can reach forward but struggles to slide the arm into a jacket sleeve. Gentle external rotation stops early. The therapist measures the movement and asks whether the shoulder feels stiff, painful, weak or unstable.
story.clinicalDecision: The elbow is supported close to the side. At the first comfortable external-rotation barrier, the patient gives a tiny isometric effort toward internal rotation while the therapist matches it. 'Ten percent effort, not a gym personal best.' After relaxation, they explore the new easy range.
story.retest: The jacket movement is checked again, then paired with active rotation and scapular control. Any improvement matters because of function—not because the therapist says a muscle 'released'.
story.punchline: The patient is the engine. The clinician is the steering, not the accelerator.
story.evidenceCaveat: Evidence for shoulder MET is mixed. A 2025 review of Spencer MET reported some functional benefit but inconsistent pain and ROM advantages; it does not directly validate every shoulder-rotation variation.
